issues.legal_issue: Pending permissions and incomplete construction do not by themselves bar specific performance where the purchaser is ready and willing to perform and the seller has breached the sale agreement.
material_facts: The purchaser had agreed to buy a flat in a building that remained incomplete, and permissions and a renewed lease were still required for the building’s completion.
The trial court and appellate court found that the purchaser had been ready and willing to perform her part of the agreement and that the seller had breached it.
The purchaser had sought specific performance promptly and was not responsible for the delay in the proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled to specific performance notwithstanding the outstanding permissions and incomplete construction, subject to the other conditions specified in the judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, specific performance is discretionary but the discretion must be exercised judicially; the circumstances in subsections (2) and (3) are not exhaustive, and subsection (4) removes mutuality as a requirement. In contracts for the sale of immovable property, specific performance is ordinarily granted and refusal requires valid and cogent grounds. Delay caused by court proceedings is not by itself a ground to refuse relief absent compelling circumstances.

rule.if: specific_performance_appeal and purchaser_ready_willing and seller_breached_agreement and purchaser_not_responsible_for_delay and (permissions_pending or construction_incomplete)

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable property.
predicates.purchaser_ready_willing: The purchaser was ready and willing to perform the purchaser’s obligations under the agreement.
predicates.seller_breached_agreement: The seller failed to perform the seller’s obligations under the agreement.
predicates.purchaser_not_responsible_for_delay: The purchaser did not cause the delay in the proceedings.
predicates.permissions_pending: Permissions or other approvals needed for the property’s completion had not yet been obtained.
predicates.construction_incomplete: Construction of the building or property remained incomplete.

issues.definition: When an appeal seeks specific performance and the purchaser was ready and willing, the seller breached the agreement, the purchaser did not cause the delay, and permissions remain pending or construction is incomplete, the rule outputs that specific performance is granted.

issues.legal_issue: Escalation in property prices and delay caused by court proceedings do not, without case-specific equitable grounds, justify requiring the purchaser to pay additional compensation as a condition of specific performance.
material_facts: The agreed price for the flat was Rs. 60,000, and the purchaser had consistently been ready and willing to perform her part of the agreement.
The purchaser had not caused the delay; the seller had sought to avoid the agreement.
The market value of the flat had risen substantially, but the purchaser had not offered to pay additional compensation.
The proposed additional payment of Rs. 40 lakhs might frustrate the agreement because the purchaser might not be able to pay it.
In the cited case of Gobind Ram, additional compensation had been directed on a concession by the purchaser; the court did not treat that result as a universal rule.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled to specific performance at the price stated in the agreement, without the additional Rs. 40 lakhs being imposed as a condition.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary, but the discretion must be exercised on sound judicial principles. Escalation in price is not by itself a universal ground to refuse specific performance or to require additional compensation; the result depends on the circumstances of the case. In Gobind Ram v. Gian Chand, additional compensation was ordered on the purchaser’s concession. K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan concerned prolonged inaction by the purchaser coupled with a substantial rise in prices. V. Pechimuthu v. Gowrammal recognized that a rise in price may be relevant when the court is considering whether to grant specific performance for the first time.

predicates.purchaser_ready_willing: The purchaser was ready and willing to perform the purchaser’s obligations under the agreement.
predicates.purchaser_not_responsible_for_delay: The purchaser did not cause the delay in the proceedings.
predicates.seller_attempted_to_avoid_agreement: The seller sought to escape performance of the agreement.
predicates.property_prices_escalated: The value of the property increased after the agreement was made.
predicates.purchaser_did_not_offer_additional_compe: The purchaser did not offer to pay compensation over and above the agreed price.
predicates.additional_payment_may_frustrate_agreeme: Requiring an additional payment might prevent the purchaser from completing the purchase and thereby defeat the agreement.

issues.definition: When, in an appeal seeking specific performance, the purchaser was ready and willing, did not cause the delay, and did not offer additional compensation, while the seller tried to avoid the agreement, prices rose, and an added payment might defeat the agreement, the rule outputs that additional compensation is not required.
